```{r include=FALSE,echo=FALSE}
require(tidyverse)
require(tigerstats)
require(MASS)
veggy <- cabbages
```

# Introduction

<!--In this section you explain what you are trying to show.  Where did the data come from?  What is the research or other question you are trying to answer?!-->
The purpose of this report is to determine whether there is a difference in average vitamin C content between cultivation methods C39 and C52. The data comes from the cabbages dataset in the MASS package.

### Is there a difference in average VitC between c39 and c52 cultivation methods?  

# Methods

<!--Decide on your methods:  use "variable analysis" or other appropriate descriptors.  Make sure to choose at least one graphical method and at least one numerical method.!-->

The explanatory variable is the cultivation method (Cult), which is categorical. The response variable is vitamin C content (VitC), which is numerical. We will use a boxplot, numerical summaries, and a two-sample t-test to determine whether there is a statistically significant difference between the two cultivation methods.

# Results

<!--Divide this section into two sub-sections:  One for your descriptive  results and one for your inferential results.!-->

## Descriptive Results

### Graphical Descriptive Results

<!--Graphical results here.  Make sure to show your code.  Provide appropriate labels for axes, giving units if possible, and provide a good title for the graph, too.  Use the graphical results to describe the patterns if any that exist in the data as focused toward the research question!-->

```{r}
boxplot(VitC ~ Cult, data=veggy,
        main="Vitamin C Content by Cultivation Method",
        xlab="Cultivation Method",
        ylab="Vitamin C (mg per 100 g)",
        col=c("lightgreen", "lightblue"))
```
The boxplot shows that cultivation method C52 has a higher median vitamin C content than cultivation method C39. C52 also has greater variability in vitamin C content.


### Numerical Descriptive Results

<!--Numerical results go here. Use the numerical results to describe the patterns if any that exist in the data as focused toward the research question!-->
```{r}
favstats(VitC ~ Cult, data=veggy)
```
The numerical summary shows that cultivation method C39 has a mean vitamin C content of 51.5 mg per 100 g, while C52 has a mean of 64.4 mg per 100 g. C52 produces cabbages with an average of 12.9 mg more vitamin C per 100 g than C39. Both cultivation methods have a sample size of 30 cabbages.

## Inferential Results

<!--State hypothesis clearly.  Make sure your discussion of the inferential test covers all the aspects that the test output produces, such as test statistic, p-value etc.  Make a decision about the null hypothesis, explain the assumptions on which the selected test/procedure was based, and why the chosen procedure satisfys the assumptions and is appropriate to answer the research question!-->

$H_0$ There is no difference in mean vitamin C content between cultivation methods C39 and C52.

$H_A$ There is a difference in mean vitamin C content between cultivation methods C39 and C52.

```{r}
t.test(VitC ~ Cult, data=veggy)
```
A Welch two-sample t-test was conducted to determine whether there is a statistically significant difference in mean vitamin C content between the two cultivation methods. The significance level is 0.05.

The Welch two-sample t-test resulted in a t-statistic of -6.3909, 56.376 degrees of freedom, and a p-value of 0.00000003405. Since the p-value is less than 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis. The 95% confidence interval ranges from -16.94 to -8.86 for the difference between C39 and C52. Since the confidence interval does not contain zero, the results are statistically significant.

The Welch two-sample t-test is appropriate because we are comparing the means of a numerical variable between two separate cultivation groups. Both groups have a sample size of 30, which supports the approximate normality of the sampling distributions. The Welch t-test does not require equal variances. However, the test assumes that the observations are independent.

# Discussion and Conclusion

The results provide sufficient statistical evidence to conclude that there is a difference in average vitamin C content between cultivation methods C39 and C52. Cultivation method C52 produces cabbages with a higher average vitamin C content of 64.4 mg per 100 g compared to 51.5 mg per 100 g for C39. Therefore, C52 appears to be the better cultivation method for producing cabbages with higher vitamin C content. However, other factors, such as growing conditions and planting dates, may also influence vitamin C content. Without additional information about the experimental design, we cannot conclude that the cultivation method alone caused the difference.
